newsitem.title: UK: COURT HEARS SOCCER STAR FELL FOR BRIBES 'STING'.
newsitem.headline: COURT HEARS SOCCER STAR FELL FOR BRIBES 'STING'.

text.p: The prosecution in England's first soccer fixing trial for 30 years has finished outlining its case against Bruce Grobbelaar, portraying the star as a man who tried to rig at least four matches.
Chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith said the former Liverpool goalkeeper had agreed to try to influence the results of the game to benefit a Far Eastern betting syndicate.

On Wednesday, a court in Winchester, southern England, heard that a newspaper obtained video evidence of Grobbelaar talking with business partner Chris Vincent -- who will be the main prosecution witness -- about fixing games.

The court was told that Vincent secretly taped Grobbelaar taking 2,000 pounds ($3,350) as an advance payment from an imaginary second syndicate in a "sting" set up by the Sun newspaper. The top-selling tabloid broke the story in November 1994.
Grobbelaar is accused along with former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, soccer-star-turned-television-presenter John Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim.
All the defendants have pleaded not guilty. They face up to seven years in jail if they are convicted.
The prosecution said Grobbelaar decided to fix the outcome of games after becoming bitter about younger players earning more than him at Liverpool.
Calvert Smith said three of Grobbelaar's four attempts to ensure Liverpool lost actually failed.

In at least one game, after his transfer to Southampton, it was alleged that he let in a goal deliberately, but his team still won. When Liverpool met Manchester United in January 1994, he saved two shots inadvertently and again his side failed to lose.

"Do you know how much money I lost? 125,000 pounds in cash," Grobbelaar is alleged to have told Vincent. He had earlier received 40,000 pounds from the syndicate when Liverpool lost 3-0 to Newcastle in late 1993, according to the prosecution.

The prosection's case is based largely on phone bills listing frequent calls between the defendants, especially around match days, and on details of bank accounts, plus covert video and audio recordings made by Vincent.

Dutchman Segers, a much less well-known footballer despite his seven years at Wimbledon, told police that large deposits into his bank account were not the proceeds of match-fixing but of car thefts he committed as a youth.
The money, he claimed, had been left in a Jersey bank account since the 1970s. Puzzled police had found no evidence of that bank account.
